text.p: THE PROTEUS COLUMN
Alternative risk finance has rarely been out of the headlines in the past few months and it is becoming clear that even when it is not making the news, ART is still taking huge steps forward.

While mergers such as Winterthur and Credit Suisse, which when coupled with the companies' existing joint venture with Swiss Re will make one of the world's most powerful alternative risk finance units, continue to take place, the pace of development cannot be slowed.

The most significant public development of recent days was the $100 million multi-year Catastrophe Equity Put (CatEPut). Developed by Aon, it allows Bermuda-based Lasalle Re to infuse up to $100 million of equity in the event of a major catastrophe.
The deal is significant because for the first time there are two CatEPut option writers, European Re, part of Swiss Re New Markets, and Allianz.

The CatEPut provides a reinstatement of funds by the option writer following a loss event in the same way a reinsurance contract would. But, instead of paying annual reinsurance premiums in the years before the loss event, the option buyer repays the capital infusion after the event.
The total amount paid is usually significantly less than would be paid in annual premiums and there is a useful tax advantage.

The option writer gains preference shares in the buyer's company. However, it loses the annual cash inflows that would come from premiums on a reinsurance contract. It also affects the liquidity of capital on the books.

Syndication of such deals means they are no longer restricted to highly capitalised reinsurers. At the same time other companies are developing products with precisely the same goal -- to attract non-insurance capital. Those on the target list include life insurers, mutual funds, hedge funds and almost any other institutional investor.
Hedge Financial Products has put together a handful of swap deals targeted specifically at attracting hedge funds and investment funds.

The deals have not been publicised -- in the same way that Aon refuses to give details of the raft of products that it has under development. These companies are not alone in their desire to hold on to their competitive advantage.

While the public face of alternative risk finance is one where insurance giants are testing the market with one or two small-scale products, complex financial engineering and new product development are being conducted at an accelerating pace behind the scenes.
The sophisticated financial products which emerge provide an efficient low-cost alternative to reinsurance and are challenging the very basis of traditional cover.

Reinsurers are increasingly finding themselves trapped in an impossible situation. While rates are low they have to write more business for less profit, and rates are unlikely to increase while so many competitive products are on offer.
At the same time, while they can gain business from entering into alternative risk financing transactions, they will lose the capital in-flows which ensure their liquidity.

The time when reinsurers are no longer risk takers but sophisticated financial engineers capable of balancing an increasingly complex portfolio of business between the traditional and the non-traditional is closer than many would care to imagine.
